text: Everything so far in this chapter has lived inside one AWS account. Real organizations usually run several, and this lesson covers the service that ties them together — AWS Organizations — along with management versus member accounts, Organizational Units, and the guardrail policies that apply across all of them.

Most companies split workloads into separate accounts on purpose: a production account for live, customer-facing systems, a development account as a sandbox developers can experiment in freely, and a security account dedicated to audit logging. Separate accounts give each workload a hard boundary — a mistake or a breach in development genuinely cannot spill into production, because they're different accounts with different resources and different billing.

AWS Organizations manages all of those accounts centrally. Every Organization has exactly one management account, which creates or invites the member accounts, hosts consolidated billing for all of them, and is the only account that can perform certain Organization-level actions. Every member account still keeps its own root user and its own IAM users, groups, and roles — Organizations adds a layer on top, it doesn't replace anything inside an account. To keep a long list of accounts manageable, they get grouped into Organizational Units, containers that can nest into a tree starting from the Organization's root — a different root entirely from the root user covered back in Lesson 1.

A Service Control Policy, attached to an OU or an account, sets the maximum permissions available to everything under it, including that account's own root user. That's what makes an SCP different from the IAM policies in Lesson 2: an IAM policy grants permissions, while an SCP only restricts what's possible in the first place. This SCP denies cloudtrail:StopLogging across an entire OU, so no account under it — not even its root user — can switch off its own audit trail.

That closes out identities and account structure. Chapter 2 moves from who can act in an AWS account to what they actually build — starting with Lesson 5, launching and sizing your first real EC2 instance.
